intro: Lawyers lose billable hours to admin work in small pieces, not in one big block. A 2017 Clio survey put administrative tasks at 48% of the average lawyer's day, and 2025 figures still show about 3 billable hours in an eight-hour day. This guide covers what the lost time costs, why it keeps happening, and fixes that need no new purchase.
tldr: Lawyers lose billable hours to admin work in small pieces across the whole day.
Clio's 2025 data, as summarized by Align, has the average lawyer billing 3.0 hours in an eight-hour day.
Measure one working week first, then fix the biggest drain with tools you already have on your Mac.
Lazur can point, guide, explain and draft while you work, but it does not do the work for you.

blocks.text: What the numbers say about lost billable time

Start with the number that controls your calendar. Clio's 2025 Legal Trends Report, as summarized by Align, has the average lawyer billing 3.0 hours in an eight-hour workday. That is a 38% utilization rate. After write-offs, the invoiced figure drops to 2.6 hours. Utilization is simply the share of your logged time that you can bill. Clio's own page would not open for us, so treat these figures as secondhand until you check the original.

A second 2025 figure points the same way. Bloomberg Law's Attorney Workload Survey, also summarized by Align, has lawyers logging 48 hours a week, with 36 of them billable. That is about 75%. The two studies measure different things, and the Bloomberg sample is described only as large firms. Read them as a range, not as a target you must hit.

Other write-ups give different figures for the same Clio 2025 data, and we could not open those pages. We use the Align figures here. If a number matters for a budget or a pitch, go to the original report and quote it from there.
Where the average lawyer's day goes

The most-cited breakdown is older, but it is still the clearest picture we have. Clio's 2017 Legal Trends Report, summarized by National Jurist, found that administrative tasks took 48% of the average lawyer's day. Business development and finding new clients took 33%. Utilization was 29%, which is about 2.3 billable hours in an eight-hour day. After realization and collection, that falls to about 1.6 hours. The figures came from more than 60,000 Clio users and a survey of 2,915 legal professionals.

blocks.caption: Clio's 2017 split of an eight-hour day, as summarized by National Jurist.

blocks.text: Read the table with one caution. The categories overlap in real life. A call with a prospective client counts as business development and also as a file note. I did not find a newer study that measures this exact split. Treat the table as a pattern to test against your own week, not as a benchmark you must match.
What lost billable hours cost you

The cost shows up in three places: money you never invoice, hours that spill into nights and weekends, and your health. The money part is easy to miss. It never appears as an expense. It appears as work you did and could not bill. Align's summary of BigHand's 2025 data says 31% of firms report lawyers doing more administrative work than a year earlier. Align also estimates lost billable time at up to $192,000 per partner per year. That estimate is not independently verified, so use it to start a conversation, not to set a budget.
Why admin work keeps crowding out billable hours

Admin rarely grows because someone decided it should. It grows because each small task looks harmless on its own. Replying to one more email, reformatting one more document or chasing one more signature each takes a few minutes. Together they fill the day. The causes below are the ones the research points to, with a caution: few studies measure cause and effect directly.
Why unbilled work stays invisible

Thomson Reuters Institute defines non-billable and unbilled time but does not measure it, as its August 2024 article notes. That gap in measurement matters. You manage what you track. If your admin hours appear in no report, they will not come up in a planning meeting. You have to make them visible yourself, starting with a log you keep for one week.
Fixes you can use today without buying anything

Every fix below uses tools you already own. Most run in Apple Mail, Outlook, Word or Apple's built-in Shortcuts app. None needs a new subscription. Start with measurement, because you cannot fix what you have not counted. The order matters. Measure first, change one thing, then measure again.

Keep the first change small. A rule that sorts court notices, or a fixed time to log entries, is easier to keep than a full overhaul. After a week, check whether the change held. If it did not, adjust it or drop it. A change you keep beats a perfect plan you abandon by Wednesday.
A one-week plan that protects billable time

The plan below takes five working days. Each day adds one habit, and none asks you to change your whole practice at once. The labels set the order, not a fixed schedule. Skip a day if the week goes sideways, then pick it up the next day.
A worked example: sorting one associate's Tuesday

Here is how the fixes add up for one hypothetical associate. Their Tuesday starts with a long list of unread messages and a court notice buried in the middle. They read each message, file two, and answer a client question that needed a quick call. Before lunch they realize the morning was never logged. They rebuild it from memory and write vague entries, such as review and call.

The fix is small. A rule sends routine messages to their own folder, so the court notice stands out. A fixed time to log, with entries written in plain words, cuts the rebuilding. A dictated file note takes less time than typing one. None of these changes adds an hour to the day. They stop the same hour from leaking away. Judge the change over a week, not a single morning, because one morning is noise.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. It lives in the notch. Hold Option and Command together to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. It points at things, guides you one click at a time, and drafts or types text. It does not click buttons or operate your apps for you, and it is not a plugin for any app. It can walk you through a rule, but you still make the rule.

items: Good fit: finding a setting you cannot locate in Apple Mail or Outlook.
Good fit: explaining a rule condition in plain words before you save it.
Good fit: drafting a routine client update that you read before you send it.
Good fit: dictating a file note while the call is still fresh.
Not a fit: anything that needs Lazur to click, send or file for you, because it does not operate apps.

blocks.text: Client data and firm rules come first

Lawyers handle privileged and confidential client information every day. Before you use any AI tool on a matter file, follow your firm's policy and your employer's rules. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot are sent to AI providers to answer and are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Those facts do not override your firm's rules, so check with your compliance or IT team first.

blocks.title: Check before you dictate client names
blocks.text: Dictation and screenshots can capture client names, matter numbers and privileged content. Close files you do not need open before you hold a shortcut. If your firm bans AI tools on client work, do not use them on that work, even for admin tasks.
Mistakes people make when they fix admin work

items: Fixing everything in one weekend. Pick one drain, fix it for a full week, then move on.
Setting rules without testing them. A rule that sends a court notice to the wrong folder costs more than it saves.
Logging time in vague words. Vague entries invite write-offs and questions from the client.
Measuring an unusual week. A trial week or a holiday skews the log, so pick a normal one.
Treating a new app as the fix. Each new app adds a login, a notification and another step.
Skipping the reread. Dictated or drafted text needs your review before it leaves your desk.
Taking studies as a benchmark. They use different samples, so use them to ask better questions.

blocks.text: How to know the fix worked

Track the same three numbers each week, in the same format. The first is your logged hours. The second is the share of those hours you billed. The third is how many entries you had to rewrite. Compare each week with the one before it. A good change should make the day feel less rushed, and the numbers should show it too.
What the research does not prove

The evidence has limits. The 48% split is from 2017, and the Clio 2025 figures reached us through a summary. The one controlled trial on AI and productivity used law students, not practicing lawyers. The University of Minnesota Law magazine reports productivity gains from 34 to 140 percent, with mixed accuracy. Check every AI output before it reaches a client.

A Thomson Reuters survey of more than 2,200 legal, tax and risk professionals found respondents expect AI to save 12 hours a week within five years. Those are expectations, not measured savings. Save time through your own habits first, then count any AI gains only after you measure them.
What to do next

Pick one drain from your log and fix it this week. If email is the drain, start with the [Outlook guide for lawyers](/for/lawyers/outlook) or the [Apple Mail page](/apps/apple-mail). If document review eats your afternoons, the [Word guide for lawyers](/for/lawyers/word) covers Track Changes, Compare and faster clause review. When you want help while you work, [download Lazur](/download) for your Mac. Lazur starts with a trial that needs no credit card, and the [pricing page](/pricing) lists current plans.

faq.question: How many billable hours does the average lawyer log in a day?
faq.answer: Align's summary of Clio's 2025 Legal Trends Report puts the average lawyer at 3.0 billable hours in an eight-hour day, a 38% utilization rate. After write-offs, that is 2.6 hours. Other write-ups give different figures, so check the original report before you quote one.

faq.question: Is the 48% admin figure still accurate?
faq.answer: It comes from Clio's 2017 Legal Trends Report, as summarized by National Jurist. It is the most-cited split we found, but it is nearly a decade old. Use it as a pattern, then measure your own week to see where the time goes.

faq.question: What does utilization mean for a lawyer?
faq.answer: Utilization is the share of your logged time that you can bill. A 38% rate means about three of every eight logged hours were billable in Clio's 2025 data. Your own number depends on your practice and on how you log time.

faq.question: Does Quick Steps work in Outlook on Mac?
faq.answer: Microsoft's Quick Steps article covers Windows, Outlook.com and Microsoft 365 versions. It does not mention Mac. Check Outlook Help on your Mac to see what your version supports, and use rules and templates if Quick Steps is missing.

faq.question: Does Lazur do the admin for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur points, guides, explains, answers out loud, and drafts or types text. It does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you. You still send the email and file the document.

faq.question: Can I use AI on client files?
faq.answer: Only if your firm's policy and your employer's rules allow it. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer and are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Those facts do not override your firm's rules.

faq.question: Is Lazur available on Windows?
faq.answer: No. Lazur runs on macOS, on both Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, not available.

faq.question: Why do some vendors quote 12 hours saved a week?
faq.answer: Thomson Reuters surveyed more than 2,200 legal, tax and risk professionals in July 2024. Respondents expect AI to save 12 hours a week within five years. Those are self-reported expectations, not measured savings.

problem: admin work crowding out billable time

costs.title: Hours you worked and could not bill
costs.text: Align's summary of Clio's 2025 data has the average lawyer billing 3.0 hours in an eight-hour day. After write-offs, that drops to 2.6 hours. The gap is work you did and could not invoice. Write-offs are easier to justify when an entry is vague or logged late. Writing entries the same day leaves fewer gaps to explain.

costs.title: Nights and weekends
costs.text: Bloomberg Law's 2025 survey, summarized by Align, has lawyers logging 48 hours a week with 36 billable. That leaves a gap of about 12 hours a week for non-billable work. The ABA and Krill Strategies study links 71 or more hours a week to much higher stress and burnout risk than a standard 40-hour week.

costs.title: Burnout and people leaving
costs.text: In the ABA and Krill Strategies study of about 37,000 actively licensed lawyers from 28 jurisdictions, 47.4% screened positive for high burnout. 15.6% met the threshold for severe burnout. 27% had considered leaving the profession because of mental health, burnout or stress. Admin overload is one pressure among several, but it is one you can change.

costs.title: Less time for new clients
costs.text: Clio's 2017 data found that 41% of law firms would spend even more of their day seeking clients if they had extra time. Admin work takes the hours that would otherwise go to business development. Slow admin does more than shrink this month's bill. It also thins out next year's pipeline.

causes.title: Billable targets reward hours, not the work around them
causes.text: Thomson Reuters Institute frames the problem around billable-hour targets. Most lawyers report billing about 1,800 hours a year. The Institute says a realistic maximum is about 3,120 hours a year, which is 60 hours a week for 52 weeks, and that very few reach it. When a target counts only billed time, admin gets no line of its own. It gets squeezed into whatever hours are left.

causes.title: Admin moves onto lawyers
causes.text: BigHand's 2025 data, as summarized by Align, found 31% of firms say lawyers do more administrative work than a year earlier. When support roles shrink or get reassigned, the tasks drift to the busiest person in the room. Make a list of the admin you now own that someone else used to handle. That list shows you where the hours went.

causes.title: Unbilled work hides in small gaps
causes.text: A quick call, a file note, a reformatted exhibit. None of these shows up unless you write it down. Thomson Reuters Institute defines non-billable and unbilled time but does not measure it. That matches most people's experience. If a task is not logged, your records treat it as if it never happened.

causes.title: Long hours make admin feel normal
causes.text: The ABA and Krill study links 71 or more hours a week to much higher stress and burnout risk. Long days make routine admin feel like a fact of life. You stop asking whether a task needs you at all. A task that could take a few minutes takes far longer when you are tired.

causes.title: Each tool adds steps
causes.text: Email, document storage, time tracking and e-signature each ask for their own logins and clicks. The steps look small. Across a week they become overhead that never appears on an invoice. Fewer, better-set-up tools often beat adding one more app to the stack.

fixes.title: Measure one working week before you change anything
fixes.text: Keep a plain log for one working week. Write down each block of time, what it was for, and whether you billed it. Use Apple Notes or a spreadsheet, whichever you open first. Look for the three tasks that took the longest and billed the least. Guesses about where time goes are often wrong, so the log is worth the effort.

fixes.title: Log time at a fixed time each day
fixes.text: Logging once a day beats a Friday catch-up. Pick a fixed slot, such as just before lunch and just before you leave. Set a repeating reminder in Apple Reminders. Describe each entry the way the client would want to read it, in plain words. Vague entries invite write-offs. Plain entries are quicker to write while the work is still fresh.

fixes.title: Sort routine mail with Apple Mail rules
fixes.text: Apple Mail can file messages before you read them. Open Mail > Settings > Rules, then choose Add Rule. Make one rule for newsletters, one for court or docket notices, and one for messages from your billing system. Send each to its own folder. Test every rule on a single message first, or a notice could land in the wrong place.

fixes.title: Use Outlook rules and templates before counting on Quick Steps
fixes.text: Microsoft's Quick Steps article covers one-click, multi-step actions on Windows, Outlook.com and New Outlook for Windows. It does not mention Mac. Check Outlook Help on your Mac before you plan around Quick Steps. Rules and saved templates are the safer starting point, and you can search Help for both.

fixes.title: Turn repeated steps into a Shortcut
fixes.text: Apple's Shortcuts guide says shortcuts run multi-step tasks across your apps, with a click or by asking Siri. Open Shortcuts and choose File > New Shortcut, or press ⌘N. Build the steps you repeat, such as copying a matter name into a standard note. The guide also has an Automations section for tasks that start on their own.

fixes.title: Dictate the notes you keep putting off
fixes.text: File notes, time descriptions and short internal updates are often faster to speak than to type. Dictate the facts in order, then read the result before it goes anywhere. Keep a short list of names and matter terms so the words come out right. Your firm's rules on client data still apply to everything you say out loud.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Measure the drains
plan.text: Keep your log for the whole day. At the end, mark the three tasks that took the longest and felt least like lawyering. Change nothing yet. Write the three down where you will see them tomorrow.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Fix your time entries
plan.text: Pick a fixed time to log. Write each entry as the client would want to read it. Put a repeating reminder in Apple Reminders for that slot, and keep the slot short enough that you will not skip it.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Sort routine mail
plan.text: Create one or two rules in Apple Mail or Outlook, starting with the messages you open but never act on. Test each rule on one message. Check that the message landed in the right folder before you trust the rule.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Build one Shortcut
plan.text: Choose the repeated step that costs you the most. Build it in Shortcuts with File > New Shortcut, or press ⌘N. Run it three times on real work, and fix what breaks before you rely on it.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Protect one admin block
plan.text: Book one admin block on your calendar for next week, at a time you can realistically keep. Put billable work in the blocks around it. Compare your log with Day 1 and note what changed.
